scope.label: Bronisław Kaper early career, documented through 1939

records.title: Birth
records.label: 5 Feb 1902 · Birth in Warsaw
records.shortDescription: Born in Warsaw to Szmul Moszek Kaper and Maria Mucha, in a Jewish family registered in the city’s non-Christian civil records.
records.longDescription: Born on January 23 (February 5, New Style) in Warsaw. Father – Szmul Moszek (later Stanisław/Samuel) Kaper, bookkeeper, aged 28. Mother – Maria (Mariam) née Mucha, aged 24. The family is of Jewish faith (registered at the Office of Civil Status for Non-Christian Confessions, 8th Jerusalem District, Warsaw).

records.title: Graduation from a primary school
records.label: 1915 · Skrynnikov school graduation
records.shortDescription: Kaper completes his early schooling at the private Skrynnikov school in Warsaw.
records.longDescription: Graduates from Skrynnikov private school in Warsaw.

records.title: High school graduation
records.label: 1919 · Staszic Gymnasium graduation
records.shortDescription: Kaper graduates from Warsaw’s Staszic Gymnasium and receives his matura certificate.
records.longDescription: Graduates from the Staszic Gymnasium in Warsaw and receives his diploma (matura certificate).

records.title: Formal matriculation at the University of Warsaw
records.label: 6 Feb 1920 · Formal UW matriculation
records.shortDescription: After the one-semester delay documented separately, Kaper was formally entered in the Faculty of Law album at the University of Warsaw.
records.longDescription: This event now records the formal matriculation rather than the earlier October 1919 application. Kaper was entered in the Faculty of Law and Political Sciences album on 6 February 1920, under album number 6854.

records.title: Baptism
records.label: 17 July 1920 · Baptism
records.shortDescription: Kaper is baptized at St. Alexander’s parish in Warsaw, marking his conversion to Catholicism.
records.longDescription: On July 17, Kaper is baptized at the Roman Catholic Parish of St. Alexander in Warsaw, at the age of 18. The baptism marks his conversion from Judaism to Catholicism.

records.title: War
records.label: 1920 · Polish–Soviet War service
records.shortDescription: Kaper serves as a volunteer in the Polish–Soviet War before returning to university life.
records.longDescription: Serves as a volunteer in the Polish-Soviet War in the rank of Senior Private (starszy szeregowy) in the Reserve Depot (Skadrowany Zapasowy) of the 1st Reconnaissance Aviation Regiment (1. Pułk Lotniczy Wywiadowczy), stationed at Mokotów, Warsaw. On November 5, he is granted indefinite leave as an "academic volunteer" (akademik ochotnik), allowing him to resume his university studies.

records.title: Music studies at the Chopin Music School in Warsaw
records.label: c. 1920–1925 · Music studies in Warsaw
records.shortDescription: Kaper studies piano and composition in Warsaw while building a strong theoretical musical foundation.
records.longDescription: His training includes piano, theory, harmony, counterpoint, composition, form, and orchestration. Achieves exceptional theoretical knowledge - able to identify complex harmonies and progressions by ear alone.

records.title: First composition
records.label: 1923 · First composition
records.shortDescription: Kaper composes his first serious composition entitled Rozmowa (Conversation) – a concert song for voice and piano.
records.longDescription: Kaper composes his first serious composition entitled Rozmowa (Conversation) – a concert song for voice and piano.

records.title: Application to Faculty of Philosophy
records.label: 1924 · Faculty of Philosophy application
records.shortDescription: Kaper seeks to transfer from law to the humanities, while taking academic leave.
records.longDescription: In September, applies for transfer to the Faculty of Philosophy, Humanities Section. The immatriculation committee conditionally accepts him, pending a certificate of departure from the Faculty of Law. Takes academic leave for the winter and summer semesters of 1923/24.

records.title: Official completion of law studies
records.label: Feb–May 1925 · Law studies completed
records.shortDescription: Kaper completes his law studies, passing the final exam and receiving formal university documents.
records.longDescription: On February 14, passes the judicial exam (egzamin prawno-sądowy) — the final of three required examinations — with a grade of "satisfactory" (dostateczny). On March 14, the Faculty of Law issues diploma no. 124. On May 26, receives his Certificate of Departure (Świadectwo Wystąpienia) no. 944.

records.title: Public performance at the Chopin Music School concert
records.label: 1925 · Chopin School public performance
records.shortDescription: Kaper performs Chopin in a public concert as a pupil of Józef Śmidowicz’s piano class.
records.longDescription: In June, appears at a public concert of the Fryderyk Chopin Higher School of Music at the Warsaw Philharmonic as a pupil of Józef Śmidowicz’s piano class. Performs the first movement of Chopin’s Piano Concerto in F minor. Warsaw critics note his “light finger technique” and “elegance combined with concentrated lyricism,”

records.title: First cabaret songs published
records.label: 1926 · First cabaret songs
records.shortDescription: Kaper’s first Warsaw cabaret songs appear under the pseudonym Bruno Asper.
records.longDescription: Songs for Warsaw cabarets published under the pseudonym Bruno Asper (lyrics by Andrzej Włast).

records.title: Move to Berlin
records.label: c. 1926 · Move to Berlin
records.shortDescription: Kaper leaves Warsaw for Berlin to continue his musical education and professional development.
records.longDescription: Leaves Warsaw for Berlin to continue music education.

records.title: Private study and first Berlin networks
records.label: 1926–1930 · Berlin study and networks
records.shortDescription: Kaper builds his Berlin career through private study with Moriz Mayer-Mahr and Walther Gmeindl, early publications, and collaboration with Fritz Rotter.
records.longDescription: After moving to Berlin, Kaper developed his professional position through private study with pianist Moriz Mayer-Mahr and composer-conductor Walther Gmeindl, while also entering the German-language song market through Fritz Rotter and early publications under the title “Dr. Kaper.”

records.title: Marriage
records.label: 30 June 1927 · Marriage in Berlin
records.shortDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora Sirot in Berlin.
records.longDescription: Kaper marries Eleonora de domo Sirot in Berlin on June 30.

records.title: Róża Etkin performs Kaper’s Sonatina in Berlin
records.label: 1927 · Etkin performs Sonatina
records.shortDescription: Róża Etkin performs Kaper’s Sonatina in Berlin, a performance later confirmed by Kaper’s oral-history recollection.
records.longDescription: A 1927 German press notice documents the Berlin performance context, and Kaper’s later oral-history recollection identifies the work as his Sonatina.

records.title: Jazz Piano Partnership
records.label: 1928 · Jazz piano partnership
records.shortDescription: Kaper records jazz-influenced piano-duo arrangements with Hermann Biek, credited on the recordings as Hermann Bick, for Polydor.
records.longDescription: Together with pianist Hermann Biek, credited on recordings as Hermann Bick, Kaper records two-piano arrangements for Deutsche Grammophon/Polydor. The documented repertoire includes American popular songs such as “Miss Annabelle Lee” and “The Song Is Ended.”

records.title: Performance of piano pieces
records.label: 1928 · Piano pieces performed in Warsaw
records.shortDescription: Eliza Rozenblum performs three unidentified piano pieces by Kaper at the Warsaw Conservatory Hall.
records.longDescription: At the Warsaw Conservatory Hall, Eliza Rozenblum performs three piano pieces by Kaper (titles unknown).

records.title: First publications and recordings with Fritz Rotter
records.label: 1929 · Rotter publications and recordings
records.shortDescription: Kaper’s tangos and foxtrots with Fritz Rotter appear in German and Viennese editions.
records.longDescription: Tangos and foxtrots by "Dr. Kaper" published in German and Viennese editions.

records.title: Involvement in Polish cultural life in Berlin
records.label: 1929 · Polish cultural life in Berlin
records.shortDescription: Kaper remains active in Berlin’s Polish cultural life, including work with the Harmonia choir.
records.longDescription: "Kurier Warszawski" reports on a concert by the Berlin choir "Harmonia", directed by Kaper.

records.title: ERKLA-Quartett concert review in Hamborn
records.label: 10 Dec 1929 · ERKLA in Hamborn
records.shortDescription: A Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung review documents Kaper’s appearance with the ERKLA four-piano ensemble in Hamborn, alongside Giuliano Pomeranz, then performing as Julian Pomeranc, Aleksander Zakin, and Leopold Mittmann.
records.longDescription: Dr. Funk’s review “Jazz auf vier Flügeln” in the Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung, 10 December 1929, p. 12, documents an ERKLA concert in Hamborn. It names Kaper alongside Giuliano Pomeranz, then performing as Julian Pomeranc, Aleksander Zakin, and Leopold Mittmann.

records.title: Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
records.label: 1929 · Bick & Kaper at Berlin premiere
records.shortDescription: The Bick und Kaper piano duo plays at a Berlin film premiere and attracts press attention.
records.longDescription: The jazz piano duo Bick und Kaper performs at the Ufa-Theater "Universum" in Berlin, opening the premiere of "Der Adjutant des Zaren." The Rhein- und Ruhrzeitung writes: "Their technique is astonishing."

records.title: First compositions for film
records.label: 1930 · First film compositions
records.shortDescription: Kaper begins composing for cinema with music for early German sound films.
records.longDescription: Music for "Alraune", directed by Richard Oswald and "Der Korvettenkapitän" directed by Rudolf Walther-Fein

records.title: Meeting Walter Jurmann
records.label: 1931 · Meeting Walter Jurmann
records.shortDescription: Kaper meets Walter Jurmann, launching the songwriting partnership that defines his European film career.
records.longDescription: Introduced by Fritz Rotter, marking the start of the Jurmann–Kaper duo. First joint project: “Die große Attraktion,” directed by Max Reichmann. Kaper composes the hit slow fox “Du warst mir ein Roman” for Richard Tauber.

records.title: Flourishing Berlin collaboration
records.label: 1932 · Berlin collaboration flourishes
records.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper partnership flourishes across German films and popular songs.
records.longDescription: Numerous German films with Jurmann–Kaper music, including "Hochzeitsreise zu dritt", "Skandal in der Parkstraße", "Es wird schon wieder besser", "Der glückliche Herr Fünf".

records.title: Migration from Berlin via Vienna to Paris
records.label: 1933 · Berlin–Vienna–Paris migration
records.shortDescription: After Nazi persecution intensifies, Kaper and Jurmann leave Berlin and relocate toward Paris.
records.longDescription: Following Nazi persecution, Kaper and Jurmann flee Berlin after UFA terminates Jewish employees' contracts. Decisive moment: Kaper and his wife are attacked by Nazi gang on main Berlin street. Both composers relocate to Paris.

records.title: Paris period
records.label: 1933–1934 · Paris period
records.shortDescription: Kaper works in Paris for French producers, contributing songs and film music with Jurmann.
records.longDescription: About 18 months of work for French producers; film "Les Nuits moscovites" with hits like "Natascha" and "On n'aime qu'une fois"; compositions for revue Parade de France.

records.title: At the Salabert studio in Montrouge
records.label: 23 Dec 1933 · Salabert studio, Montrouge
records.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann are reported at the Salabert studio in Montrouge during a Paris recording session.
records.longDescription: "Paris-Soir" reports on Kaper and Jurmann present at the Salabert recording studio in Montrouge, where Henri Garat records songs for his latest film.

records.title: Songs beyond cinema
records.label: 22 June 1934 · Songs beyond cinema
records.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper songs move beyond cinema into the French concert and festival repertoire.
records.longDescription: Jurmann–Kaper songs enter the French concert repertoire. At a summer festival in Montpellier, a jazz orchestra performs "Ninon, quand tu me souris" from "Tout pour l'amour" on an open-air stage.

records.title: Cocktail with Jan Kiepura
records.label: 17 Feb 1934 · Cocktail with Jan Kiepura
records.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann attend a Paris reception for Jan Kiepura as composers of Tout pour l’amour.
records.longDescription: In February, Kaper attends a cocktail reception for Jan Kiepura at the George V in Paris together with Walter Jurmann. A contemporary press report names them among the invited guests and identifies them as the composers of the music for Tout pour l’amour.

records.title: European afterlife
records.label: 1934–1936 · European afterlife
records.shortDescription: Jurmann–Kaper films and songs continue circulating in Europe after the composers leave for America.
records.longDescription: While the composers head to America, their European films and songs continue to circulate. In September 1934, "Madame wird kinderlieb" still plays in Stuttgart with Jurmann and Kaper credited — despite Nazi purges. In France, "Tout pour l'amour" with Kiepura screens as late as 1936; the Journal de Vichy calls their music "infiniment plaisante."

records.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
records.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
records.shortDescription: Kaper arrives in New York from France with Eleonora, holding a temporary visa and travelling onward to Los Angeles.
records.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora arrived in New York aboard the S.S. Champlain from Le Havre on 24 October 1934, with Los Angeles listed as their destination.

records.title: Legal Permanent Entry
records.label: 1 Nov 1935 · Permanent U.S. entry
records.shortDescription: Kaper enters the United States for permanent residence through Calexico with Eleonora.
records.longDescription: Enters for permanent residence at Calexico, California, from Mexicali on 1 November 1935, travelling on foot with Eleonora. The manifest records 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood, as his U.S. destination; his Declaration of Intention four months later records the same address as his residence.

records.title: Hollywood debut
records.label: 1935 · Hollywood debut
records.shortDescription: Kaper makes his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing to Escapade and other major studio projects.
records.longDescription: First American score: "Escapade" (dir. Robert Z. Leonard) with William Powell and Luise Rainer. Press hails "Two New Composers" of Kiepura's European hits. Songs also for Marx Brothers' "A Night at the Opera" (with Ned Washington) and "Mutiny on the Bounty".

records.title: San Francisco success and Three Smart Girls
records.label: 1936 · San Francisco and Three Smart Girls
records.shortDescription: The title song from San Francisco becomes a major hit, while Kaper and Jurmann also contribute to Universal’s Three Smart Girls.
records.longDescription: The success of San Francisco made Kaper and Jurmann more visible in Hollywood and helped establish Kaper’s reputation beyond the MGM studio system. The event also includes Three Smart Girls, the Universal production associated with Deanna Durbin and Joseph Pasternak.

records.title: Declarations of Intention
records.label: 4 Feb 1936 · Declarations of Intention
records.shortDescription: Bronisław and Eleonora Kaper file Declarations of Intention to become U.S. citizens in Los Angeles.
records.longDescription: On 4 February 1936, Bronisław Kaper and Eleonora Kaper each filed a Declaration of Intention in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, Los Angeles. Bronisław Kaper’s declaration records him as residing at Château des Fleurs, 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood.

records.title: Everybody Sing with Gus Kahn
records.label: Jul 1937–Mar 1938 · Everybody Sing with Gus Kahn
records.shortDescription: Kaper and Walter Jurmann collaborate with lyricist Gus Kahn on songs for the MGM musical Everybody Sing.
records.longDescription: On 13 July 1937, The Washington Daily News reported that Gus Kahn was studying musical notation with Kaper and Jurmann while they worked on The Ugly Duckling, the working title of Everybody Sing. A Brooklyn Daily Eagle notice of 17 March 1938 documents the released film and credits songs to Kaper and Jurmann.

records.title: European Film Fund
records.label: 1938 · European Film Fund
records.shortDescription: Kaper participates in the European Film Fund, helping support refugees from the European film community.
records.longDescription: The European Film Fund was established in 1938 by Paul Kohner, Ernst Lubitsch, and Carl Laemmle to aid refugees arriving from Europe. Kaper participated in the Fund despite his relatively secure position at MGM. A surviving donor list for 1 May 1941–30 April 1942 records “Kaper, Bronislaw” and a contribution of $120, providing direct documentary evidence of his involvement.

records.title: End of an era
records.label: 1938 · Jurmann–Kaper era ends
records.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper collaboration ends amicably as Hollywood’s musical priorities change.
records.longDescription: Amicable end of Jurmann–Kaper collaboration; industry changes reduce demand for thematic songs.

records.title: New chapter
records.label: 1939 · Solo MGM chapter begins
records.shortDescription: Kaper remains at MGM and begins a new solo chapter as a film composer.
records.longDescription: Kaper remains with MGM, starting a solo career as a film composer.

records.title: University admission delayed by a disciplinary sanction
records.label: Delayed UW matriculation
records.shortDescription: Kaper’s admission to the Faculty of Law at the University of Warsaw was delayed by a one-semester disciplinary sanction before his formal matriculation in February 1920.
records.longDescription: University records show that Kaper applied to the Faculty of Law at the University of Warsaw in October 1919, but that the Matriculation Commission rejected his immediate admission after a disciplinary incident. The sanction was temporary: he later described it in his curriculum vitae as a one-semester relegation, and he was formally entered in the faculty album on 6 February 1920.

records.title: Police certificate records Mosaic religion
records.label: Mosaic religion recorded
records.shortDescription: A police certificate issued shortly before Kaper’s baptism recorded his religion as “Mosaic,” the official term then used for the Jewish faith.
records.longDescription: The certificate of good conduct issued by the Warsaw State Police forms an important documentary link between Kaper’s university records and the later baptismal entry. It anchors the discussion of identity in administrative sources rather than retrospectively imposed narratives: Kaper appears in the record as a young Warsaw student from an assimilated Jewish family whose formal confessional status changed only a few months later.

records.title: Koszutski Girls and the B. Asper pseudonym
records.label: Koszutski Girls / B. Asper
records.shortDescription: The manuscript Koszutski Girls shows Kaper already working with revue-dance conventions and using the B. Asper signature that would later appear in printed songs.
records.longDescription: Koszutski Girls complicates a simple division between Kaper’s concert training and his later popular-song career. Although preserved as an autograph manuscript, the piece is tied to Warsaw revue culture and to the international fashion for “girls” troupes. Its practical performance marking and the signature “Mus. B. Asper” foreshadow the pseudonymous popular-song activity of 1926–1927, making it a useful early marker of Kaper’s movement between concert idiom, cabaret practice, and commercial entertainment.

records.title: Entry into Warsaw popular song: Craig, Włast, and Altschuler
records.label: First Warsaw song network
records.shortDescription: Kaper later traced his entry into popular song to a Warsaw network linking “Henry Craig,” Andrzej Włast, cabaret performance, and Altschuler’s publishing house.
records.longDescription: Kaper’s own account presents the move into songwriting as accidental: a friend whom he called “Henry Craig” introduced him to a leading Warsaw lyricist identifiable as Andrzej Włast, after which the song reached the cabaret stage and then print. Read together with the surviving printed songs, this episode explains how a composer trained in concert idioms entered the commercial structures of interwar Warsaw popular song: lyricist, cabaret performer, publisher, and sheet-music circulation.

records.title: Earliest documented collaboration with Fritz Rotter
records.label: First Rotter trace
records.shortDescription: A 1926 manuscript of Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener documents an early collaboration between Kaper and Fritz Rotter, before sound film became his main professional platform.
records.longDescription: The manuscript credit for Hätt’ ich einen Kammerdiener places Kaper beside Fritz Rotter at an early point in his Berlin years. It is an important transitional event: Rotter linked Kaper to the practical economy of the German hit song—publishers, performers, promotion, and sheet-music circulation—before those skills were absorbed into the machinery of early sound film. It also explains why Rotter later became the mediator who brought Kaper and Walter Jurmann together.

records.title: Alraune as Kaper’s first documented sound-film commission
records.label: Alraune and sound film
records.shortDescription: Alraune marks Kaper’s first clearly documented entry into early sound film, through songs rather than background scoring in the later Hollywood sense.
records.longDescription: Kaper’s first documented sound-film work belongs to the early phase of cinema in which the film composer’s task was still closely tied to song production. Alraune, Richard Oswald’s 1930 sound remake, did not yet require the later Hollywood model of continuous underscoring. Instead, Kaper contributed songs that could serve the film while also entering the wider economy of printed scores, records, performers, and radio.

records.title: The Sängerfilm and the star-singer circuit
records.label: Sängerfilm circuit
records.shortDescription: Kaper and Jurmann’s songs entered the Sängerfilm economy, where screen performance, star singers, sheet music, records, radio, and dance-band repertory reinforced one another.
records.longDescription: The Kaper–Jurmann partnership developed inside the commercial ecology of early European musical film. Their songs for productions associated with singers such as Richard Tauber and Jan Kiepura were not simply film numbers: they were designed to travel beyond the screen as printed music, recordings, radio items, and repertory for performers. This star-singer circuit explains why the duo’s European experience later appeared useful to MGM, which read it through the promotional language of Viennese musical competence.

records.title: Multiple-language versions and transnational sound-film production
records.label: Transnational sound film
records.shortDescription: Before 1933, Kaper and Jurmann were already working within the multiple-language version system that linked Babelsberg, Joinville, Vienna, and other European production centres.
records.longDescription: The practice of producing parallel language versions was one of the key industrial conditions of early sound cinema. It allowed music to move more easily than dialogue across national markets, even when lyrics, singers, and performance contexts changed. Kaper and Jurmann’s work in this system gave their songs and professional skills a transnational character before their forced departure from Germany.

records.title: Ninon reaches Louis B. Mayer: the Ritz meeting and MGM contract
records.label: Ninon opens the MGM path
records.shortDescription: The European success of Ninon reportedly brought Kaper and Jurmann to the attention of Louis B. Mayer, leading to a meeting at the Hôtel Ritz and an MGM contract.
records.longDescription: Kaper later recalled that the success of Ninon—written for Tout pour l’amour, the French version of Ein Lied für Dich—was the turning point that opened the path to Hollywood. During his European talent-scouting trip in August 1934, Louis B. Mayer reportedly asked to meet the song’s authors, heard them perform at the Hôtel Ritz, and offered a seven-year MGM contract.

records.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
records.label: MGM’s “Viennese” label
records.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
records.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers” and as a brilliant Viennese musical team. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity.

records.title: Duke Ellington records “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm”
records.label: 8 Jun 1937 · Ellington records “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm”
records.shortDescription: Duke Ellington and His Famous Orchestra record “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm” in New York, carrying a Kaper–Jurmann film song into the jazz repertoire.
records.longDescription: Duke Ellington and His Famous Orchestra recorded “All God’s Chillun Got Rhythm” in New York on 8 June 1937 for Master (MA 137, matrix M 519-1). Written by Bronisław Kaper and Walter Jurmann with words by Gus Kahn for A Day at the Races, the song passed from the screen into the jazz repertoire within weeks of the film’s release.

records.title: “You’re All I Need” among the most-played songs of 1935–36
records.label: 5 Sep 1936 · “You’re All I Need” ranks 14th on the ASCAP list
records.shortDescription: Motion Picture Herald publishes the ASCAP tabulation of songs broadcast most often in 1935–36; “You’re All I Need” ranks 14th with 21,424 performances on NBC and CBS.
records.longDescription: On 5 September 1936 Motion Picture Herald printed the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers tabulation of the 112 songs performed at least 10,000 times over the NBC and CBS networks during 1935–36. “You’re All I Need,” written for Escapade, ranked 14th with 21,424 broadcasts — placing Kaper and Jurmann’s first American song among that year’s most-played titles, one year after their arrival. The list credits the film under its working title Lie Like Gentlemen and prints Jurmann’s name as “Walter Jarmann.”
